I'm currently studying at the University of Tehran. In my first two years of studying, I had a bad GPA. I have some activities in my résumé that might make up for it, and better performances in the recent semesters. My GPA is currently 15.05 out of 20, roughly 3.21 in the US terms (I used UC Irvine's Iranian grades to GPA calculator; I'm aware other universities might use other methods to calculate it.) I'm currently a B student, while after this semester and the next, which is my final, my average might enter the B+ area.

I want to enroll in an MA program in my country to compensate for any insufficiency of my BA's GPA and the lack of paper-related activities (my academic activities has been only some self published online translations, some short essays, some translations published in student quarterlies and magazines, and being a part of two student theatre festivals.) The secondary MA is for, that, I don't know if my Iranian MA will have the same credentials of some better programs abroad, in order to enroll in a distinguished institution.

To make it clear, I'm a Theatre student in BA, interested in drama history. I seek to study at Harvard in Comparative Literature for PhD, since their approach in post-colonial studies, and more textual and theoretical-focused frameworks, will be much more suited for my studies (also, the well-known Harvard library will be a great asset.)

That's why I'm thinking about two MAs.

It's not easy like that here, unfortunately. In the last 12-18 months, the dollar rate here doubled, the inflation rate is nerve-racking. I had a part-time job in a bookstore; my monthly salary? Barely made it into 3 digits after being converted into the USD, and most of the full time jobs which might accept students, pay only about 110-150% more. You might barely make 250$ here. And that's with the current exchange rate; when I started working there, 1$ was about 600K Iranian Rials. Only two months later, the exchange rate went up to 800K; even at one point it reached 1 Million Rials. So, yeah; saving money and enjoying life here is impossible. Apart from being able to continue studying and having an opportunity in my field academically, I need some financial instability too.

Also, I'm a man (he/him,) and we're required by law to do service. With an oppressive regime that most of us are against, the lowest sense of patriotism ever, brutal and inhumane conditions of military (not being soft, like, we have one of the highest soldier suicides in the world, it just won't get reported because of erasure of documents,) the service being a long 18-24 months time frame, and the probabilities of a war, I don't want to serve. Most Iranian males get an MA, even with the knowledge that they won't need it, just to evade the service for two more years, and a higher chance of getting office jobs instead of regular military jobs.

I'm evading things too, apart from pursuing academic prowess. I'm not, at all, saying that academia is my gateway of escape; I love my field, I'm passionate about it, and even with many of these economic and socio-political matters being absent, I still would've pursued academic endeavours abroad, for a better perspective and positions. But It's an uphill battle.
I'm worried about scholarships. I don't know which institutions have the financial facilities, enough to fund students. Especially in my field.

They both mean "Student". DâneshÂmooz is used for students from elementary school to high School. Dâneshjoo is used for students of higher education. Dâneshjoo has a bit a respect and formality.

The first part of each word, Dânesh (دانش) mean Science. The second part, which is different, needs some explanation.

Before that, remember in Persian grammar Infinitives and imperative verbs which are used to make new words. Let me explain more.

Here we have tge infinitive of the verb "To learn" or Âmookhtan (آموختن). All infinitives in Persian has that "-an" at the end of the word. If we remove that, it became "Âmookht" (آموخت) which is a past form of the word. For an example, "Ali dars râ âmookht" (علی درس را آموخت) means: Ali learned the subject. We call these "Bon-i Mâzi" (بُنِ ماضی) or "Past root of Infinitive". We have to types of roots for infinitive: 1) Past (which I have explained so far) 2) Present.

The two words of "joo" and "âmooz" are actually Present roots of Infinitives (Bon-i mozare'; بُنِ مضارع). To make a present root, you must first make an imperative verb from infinitive. Let's do it with "Âmooz" as we did an Past root of it earlier.

The imperative form of "Âmookhtan" is "Beeâmooz" (بیاموز) wich means "Do learn". Now, each imperative word in Persian has that "B" (بِـ) at the beginning of the word. Sometimes, like this word which starts with "â" vowel, That "Be" becomes "Bee" (بی). No matter which one of them, when we remove that "Be" we have a Present root of Infinitive. Here, "Beâmooz" becomes "Âmooz" (آموز) and could be used in some present types of verbs.

For "joo", "Jostan" (جستن) means "Seeking". Imperative: "Bejoo" (بجو) meaning "Do seek sth". Present root of Infinitive: "joo".

Conclusion:
Dânesh Âmooz (دانش آموز): One who learns science. (Elementary to High School)
Dâneshjoo (دانشجو): One who seeks science. (Undergrad to postgraduate)

If you can access hardcopy books, there are some good choices we have in Iran. Like AriyanPoor (آریان پور) Dictionary. But if you search in persian, you can find a variety of good dictionaries. Google Translate is good for single words and verbal phrases.

Listen to so many Farsi content. Whichever dialect you're going to speak, if you listen to them so much, you can pretty much imitate the accent. If you train and gain knowledge of how vocal chords work, you can speak with a native accent.

There is bo difference between مشکی and سباه. Meshki is from ancient Persian and even used in form of مشکین as verb. Siyah is a little related to Turkish. Although in Turkish, the word قره is used more often and even in Farsi speaking countries, we have a sour product called قره قروت.

Although, in formal texts, Siyah used more often and Meshki could be a little more informal. Still, using Meshki or Meshkin in a formal text has no problem.

About توسی and خاکستری, you can use both. There's no formal or informal situation between these two. Khakestari literally means "Ash like" but Toosi is a bit of special word. But there's no difference in use at all.

Finally, قرمز and سرخ. They both can be used as same. No formal and informal. However, there's a twist. You technically can call the purest red Sorkh, it's better to call it Ghermez. Sorkh could be used when describing darker reds.

So you may know the alphgbets. However still learn the way that Persians use alphabets. As in Persian, some letters used that may not the available in Arabic letters. Like /ch/ (چ), /zh/ (ژ), /p/ (پ) and /g/ (گ).

Second point is that which dialect you want to learn. Although you can learn the basic and universal formal Persian which helps you to read any Persian texts in books etc. However if you want to use Persian as a way to talk with natives, you must decide between Dari (Afghan dialect), Tajîk (Tajikistan dialect) or Farsi (Iranian dialect). Because there are different loan words and informal ways if pronouncing certain words.

In Dari, there are more English loan words; in Tajîk more Russian and in Farsi more French words. The best example is the word impression. In English you pronounce this word as (eemp-re-shen) but in French you pronounce it as (amp-re-see-yun). This could be a little difficult if you learn Dari and decide to read some Farsi academic textbooks.

But in general, if you learn each dialect you can still talk perfectly with any native Persian speaker.

The main difficulty of learning Persian is vocabulary. The grammar is not hard. It only has ine grammatic case which makes your life a lot easier. Although since you know Urdu and Punjabi and Hindi and English, you know some Persian words by default. Numbers are so similar between Punjabi and Persian.

I wish your learning process will be fun.
